claims.text: Thermal exposure activates diffusion-controlled segregation of Mg from a metastable solid solution.
Mg segregation produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Fine, uniformly dispersed Mg-rich precipitates maintain a local matrix chemistry favorable to a stable protective oxide.
Coarse or interconnected Mg-rich precipitates deplete corrosion-resistant elements from the matrix.
Coarse or interconnected Mg-rich precipitates create microgalvanic sites.
Elemental depletion and microgalvanic sites compromise corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial material is a non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase or near-single-phase lightweight HEA with Mg uniformly dissolved in the solid solution.
Thermal aging in the range of approximately 500–700 °C can induce Mg diffusion and intermetallic precipitation.
Aged specimens and unaged quenched specimens will be evaluated under identical exposure conditions as a controlled comparison.
Mg-rich intermetallics nucleate and grow at grain boundaries or within grains.
Mg-rich precipitates alter the local distribution of corrosion-inhibiting and oxidation-resisting elements in the matrix.
A fine precipitate distribution allows the matrix to retain or locally enrich elements that favor a coherent protective oxide scale.
A connected precipitate network undermines oxide-scale integrity and accelerates microgalvanic corrosion.
After thermal aging, TEM, SEM-EDS, and XRD should reveal Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Samples with fine, uniform precipitates should retain or slightly improve corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Samples with coarse or interconnected Mg-rich phases should show marked degradation of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
The proposed mechanism applies when service temperature and exposure time are sufficient for significant Mg diffusion and precipitation, approximately within 500–700 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply during rapid thermal transients or below the temperature needed to activate Mg diffusion.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and predicted outcome explicitly allow significant fine-precipitate evolution to retain or improve protective behavior, but the falsification rule presents significant precipitate evolution accompanied by retained or improved behavior as a reason for rejection. Retention or improvement is therefore both a predicted result and, as worded, a falsifying result.
